newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire students opposed to PM occupy parliament.
newsitem.headline: Zaire students opposed to PM occupy parliament.

text.p: Thousands of students demanding the resignation of part-Tutsi Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo took over Zaire's parliament building briefly on Thursday.

Witnesses said security forces did not intervene as the students, carrying the coffins of two students killed in earlier protests, flooded into the building housing the transitional national assembly. The students later dispersed peacefully.
Albertos Mupa, a student from the higher institute for applied technology, called for Kengo's resignation, saying he was a traitor.
"The noble people of Zaire have been humiliated by the aggression of Rwanda," he said.
Students in the capital, denouncing the government handling of the Tutsi revolt in eastern Zaire, had staged a series of sometimes violent protests earlier in the week.
They denounced Tutsi-led Rwanda, accused by Zaire of sending troops to fight alongside the rebels, and looted property of ethnic Tutsis in the capital.

Although the government has banned all protests, the students took over the parliament building and sat in seats of the debating chamber reserved for assembly members. They displayed the coffins on a stage at the front of the chamber.
Students said they would bury those killed in clashes with security forces on Friday.
The students, many wearing red bandanas and holding leaves symbolising peace, carried a cross with Kengo's name and Thursday's date.
Witnesses said unarmed gendarmes and unarmed troops were inside the parliament building while armed army units patrolled streets nearby.
Parliament was expected to discuss a motion of censure on Kengo's government on Thursday afternoon but witnesses said assembly members loyal to him were forced to flee before the session began.
Members loyal to radical opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi, Kengo's bitter rival, remained in the building with the students.
There have also been student protests in Kisangani in the north east, where refugees from the conflict in the east have started to arrive.
Hundreds of Tutsis, who were prominent in the business and professional community in the capital, have fled across the Zaire River to neighbouring Congo.
